- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 10–30% for early horizon (1–7 days) and 20–50% for mid/late horizon (8–30 days).  
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33), model often underestimates or fails to capture sharp declines; increase forecast for first 3–5 days by 10–20% to account for volatility.  
- After a spike in sentiment (e.g., 1.00), model frequently overshoots in the next 3–5 days; apply a “cool-down” correction: reduce forecast by 15–30% for days 4–7 post-spike.  
- Model shows strong mean reversion bias: if forecast is >2.0 for 3+ consecutive days, reduce by 10–25% for next 5 days; if <0.5, increase by 10–20% for next 3 days.  
- For horizon >15 days, model tends to ignore sentiment trends; weight sentiment history more heavily for days 1–7, then apply decay (e.g., 0.7x sentiment weight for days 8–15).  
- If sentiment history shows alternating +/– signals (e.g., 0.67, 0.33, 0.67), model often misreads trend direction; treat as “neutral” and apply conservative forecast (±5% buffer) unless sentiment is sustained >0.7 for 3+ days.
